lines.cap: Soak chopped red cabbage in warm water, and you've made a spy gadget: a purple liquid that changes colour with what it touches.
It's detecting **acids** and **alkalis**, and they're everywhere: in your kitchen, in the soil, even in your stomach.
Then there are **metals**: why do some fizz with acid, while others just sit there?
We'll measure acids with the **pH scale**, cancel them by **neutralisation**, and predict what metals do with the **reactivity series**.
An **acid** is a substance that releases **hydrogen ions**, **H⁺**, when it dissolves in water. That's what makes acids taste **sour**.
You meet acids every day: **citric acid** in lemons, and **ethanoic acid**, also called acetic acid, in vinegar.
Your stomach even makes **hydrochloric acid** to help digest food, while a layer of **mucus** protects its lining.
A **base** is the chemical opposite of an acid: it can **neutralise** an acid, cancelling it out.
Many bases are **metal oxides** or **metal hydroxides**, like copper oxide and magnesium hydroxide.
An **alkali** is a base that **dissolves in water**: a **soluble base**.
**Sodium hydroxide** is an alkali, and so is the **ammonia** in some cleaning sprays. Alkalis feel **soapy**, and many are **cleaners**.
So **all alkalis are bases**, but **not all bases are alkalis**.
**Copper oxide** doesn't dissolve in water, so it's a base, but **not** an alkali.
The **pH scale** measures how acidic or alkaline a solution is. The usual school scale runs from **0 to 14**.
Below **7** is **acidic**. The **lower** the number, the **more acidic** the solution.
At room temperature, **pure water** is exactly **pH 7**: **neutral**, neither acidic nor alkaline.
Above **7** is **alkaline**. A **higher** number means **more alkaline**, not more acidic.
The pH is linked to the concentration of **hydrogen ions**: each step **down** the scale means **ten times** more.
So lemon juice, at about **pH 2**, has around **a hundred times** the hydrogen-ion concentration of tomato juice, at about **pH 4**.
But pH doesn't tell you an acid's **strength**. A **strong** acid **ionises**, or splits into ions, **fully** in water. A **weak** acid only partly.
pH also depends on **concentration**, so you **can't** tell whether an acid is strong or weak from its pH alone.
To find a pH, use an **indicator** or a **pH meter**. Never taste or touch a chemical to find out.
An **indicator** changes **colour** with pH, so you can tell acidic, neutral and alkaline solutions apart.
**Litmus** turns **red in acid** and **blue in alkali**, but it can't give you a pH number.
Remember: **Red Bottoms, Blue Roofs**. Picture the pH scale as a tower: **red** for acids at the **bottom**, **blue** for alkalis at the **roof**.
**Universal indicator** is a **mixture of dyes**, so it shows a whole range of colours.
**Red** for about pH 0 to 2, **orange** for 3 to 4, and **yellow** for 5 to 6. All acidic.
**Green** at pH 7: **neutral**.
Then **blue** for about 8 to 11, and **purple** for 12 to 14: alkaline.
The colours are approximate, so check your indicator's **chart**. And a colour estimates **pH**, not acid strength.
**Red cabbage** juice is a **natural indicator**: **red** or pink in acids, purple near neutral, then **blue**, **green** and **yellow** as the pH climbs.
Try it at home: pour the juice into clear cups, then add **lemon juice** to one and **bicarbonate of soda** to another.
Acids taste **sour**, but never taste anything in a lab! They turn **blue litmus red**, and react with **metals** and **carbonates**.
**Alkalis** feel **soapy** or slippery, turn **red litmus blue**, and **neutralise** acids.
Check the **hazard symbol**. **Corrosive** chemicals **destroy living tissue**, like skin and eyes. Many concentrated acids and alkalis are corrosive.
**Irritants** are less severe: they cause **redness** or itching. Many **dilute** acids and alkalis are irritants.
**Dilute** means a **little** acid dissolved in **lots of water**.
**Concentrated** means **lots** of acid in **little water**.
A concentrated solution is **more hazardous**, because there are **more acid particles** in every drop.
But concentration is **not** strength. Strength is how fully an acid **ionises**; concentration is how much acid is in the water.
So you can have a **dilute strong** acid, or a **concentrated weak** acid, and the dilute strong one can be **safer**.
So always wear **safety goggles**: even a weak acid can be concentrated and harmful.
**Neutralisation** is the reaction between an **acid** and a **base**. They cancel out, moving the pH towards **7**.
With a metal oxide or hydroxide, you get a **salt** and **water**: **acid + base → salt + water**.
Remember it as **A-B-S-W**: **A**cid + **B**ase → **S**alt + **W**ater.
For example: **hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water**.
What's really happening? **Hydrogen ions**, H⁺, from the acid join **hydroxide ions**, OH⁻, from the alkali, to make **water**, H₂O.
But the **amounts** matter. Add too **little** alkali, and some acid is left over, so the solution is still **acidic**.
Add **too much**, and the extra alkali makes it **alkaline**. Mixing doesn't automatically give pH 7, so check with an **indicator**.
And neutralising isn't just diluting, or making things 'safe'. It's a **chemical reaction** that makes **new substances**: salt and water.
Farmers spread a measured amount of **lime**, a base, on **acidic soil**, so their crops grow well.
And **indigestion tablets** contain bases, like magnesium hydroxide, to neutralise **excess stomach acid**.

chapters.title: Acids and metals: the squeaky pop

lines.cap: Drop **magnesium** into dilute acid, and it **fizzes**. Those bubbles are **hydrogen** gas.
The pattern is: **acid + metal → salt + hydrogen**.
For example: **hydrochloric acid + magnesium → magnesium chloride + hydrogen**.
To **test for hydrogen**, hold a **lit splint** at the mouth of the tube. Hydrogen gives a **squeaky pop**!
It's a tiny amount of hydrogen **burning explosively**.
Time for a race: four metals in the same dilute acid.
**Magnesium** fizzes **vigorously**, with a fast stream of bubbles.
**Zinc** gives a **steady**, moderate fizz.
**Iron** fizzes only **slowly**, with bubbles forming gently.
And **copper**? **No reaction at all**, however long you wait.
That's the **reactivity series** in action: the more reactive the metal, the faster the fizz. Copper sits **below hydrogen**, so it doesn't react.
Naming the salt: the **first** part comes from the **metal**, and the **second** from the **acid**.
**Hydrochloric** acid, HCl, makes **chlorides**; **sulfuric** acid, H₂SO₄, makes **sulfates**; and **nitric** acid, HNO₃, makes **nitrates**.
So **zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfate + hydrogen**. That's sulfate, by the way, **not** sulfide.
**Metal carbonates**, like the **calcium carbonate** in chalk and limestone, fizz with acid too. But they react differently.
**acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide**
For example: **hydrochloric acid + calcium carbonate → calcium chloride + water + carbon dioxide**.
That's **three** products, and the gas is **carbon dioxide**, not hydrogen, so a lit splint won't pop. It just goes out.
To **test for carbon dioxide**, bubble it through **limewater**, a solution of calcium hydroxide. It turns **milky**, or cloudy.
The cloudiness is a fine white solid: a **precipitate** of **calcium carbonate**.
So if two powders both fizz with acid, a gas test tells them apart: a **metal** gives hydrogen, a **carbonate** gives carbon dioxide.
Remember: **Pop = Hydrogen, Milky = CO₂**.
The **reactivity series** is a league table of metals, from **most reactive** at the top to **least reactive** at the bottom.
From the top: **potassium**, **sodium**, **calcium**, **magnesium**, **aluminium**, **zinc** and **iron**.
Then **hydrogen**, and below it **copper**, **silver** and, last of all, **gold**.
To remember it: **P**lease **S**top **C**alling **M**e **A** **Z**ebra, **I**nstead **C**all **S**ome **G**old.
**Hydrogen** isn't a metal. It's a **marker**: metals above it react with acids, and metals below it don't.
The higher the metal, the more **vigorously** it reacts. **Potassium** and **sodium** react fast with **cold water**, fizzing as they release **hydrogen**.
**metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen**. So **sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen**.
The sodium hydroxide dissolves, which is why the solution left behind is **alkaline**.
Lower down, **magnesium** reacts only **slowly** with cold water, but **quickly** with **steam**.
And **copper**, **silver** and **gold** don't react with water at all.
So a metal's place in the series lets you **predict** how it will react, before you test it.
The series also predicts **displacement**: a **more reactive** metal **pushes** a less reactive one out of its compound.
Put an **iron** nail into **blue copper sulfate** solution. Iron is **more reactive**, so it pushes the copper out.
**iron + copper sulfate → iron sulfate + copper**
Watch: the **blue colour fades**, and a **brown coating of copper** appears on the nail.
But never the other way round: **copper** can't displace iron, so copper dipped into iron sulfate does **nothing**.
Most metals are found in **ores**: rocks where the metal is joined to other elements, like oxygen. Getting it out is **extraction**.
To extract **iron**, heat its ore with **carbon**. Carbon is **more reactive** than iron, so it **displaces** the iron.
**Aluminium** is more reactive than carbon. It clings to its oxygen so tightly that it needs **electrolysis**, using electricity, which is **expensive**.
And **gold** and **silver** are so unreactive that they can be found as **pure metals**, needing almost no extraction.
So **recycling** aluminium saves about **95%** of the energy, and engineers are working to run electrolysis on **renewable** electricity.
Metals react with **oxygen** in the air, too: **metal + oxygen → metal oxide**.
The oxide is a **new substance**, with different properties from the shiny metal.
Heat **magnesium**, and it burns with a dazzling, **bright white flame**, leaving a **white powder**. Never look straight at it!
That's **magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide**. In symbols: **2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO**.
**Sodium** is so reactive that a freshly cut surface **tarnishes** in seconds, as a dull layer of **sodium oxide** forms. That's why it's stored **under oil**.
**Iron** reacts more slowly. Iron filings sprinkled into a flame give **orange sparks**.
Over time, iron also combines with oxygen **and water** to form **rust**. So we protect it with paint, oil, or a coat of zinc.
And **gold**, at the bottom, doesn't react with oxygen **at all**, so a gold ring stays shiny for a lifetime.
Same pattern again: the **higher** the metal, the **more fiercely** it reacts with oxygen.
You know two gas tests already. Here's the third: **oxygen**.
Light a wooden splint, then **blow it out**, so it's only **glowing**.
Push the glowing splint into the gas. If it's oxygen, the splint **relights**, bursting back into flame!
Oxygen **supports burning**. Air is only about **a fifth** oxygen, so a tube full of it makes the splint flare back up.
So, all three tests. **Hydrogen**: a **lit** splint gives a **squeaky pop**.
**Oxygen**: it **relights** a **glowing** splint.
**Carbon dioxide**: it turns **limewater milky**.
Don't mix up the splints: **lit** for hydrogen, **glowing** for oxygen.
Salts are useful: **copper sulfate** goes into fungicides, and **ammonium nitrate** is a fertiliser.
Let's make a pure, dry sample of a **soluble salt**, copper sulfate: **copper oxide + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate + water**.
Step one: in a lab, **warm** the acid and stir in **black copper oxide**, a little at a time, until **no more reacts**.
Using **excess**, so some is left over, makes sure **all the acid is used up**, and none is left to contaminate the salt.
Step two: **filter**. The leftover copper oxide stays on the paper: the **residue**. The blue salt solution passes through: the **filtrate**.
Step three: gently **heat** the filtrate to evaporate some water, until it's **saturated**, holding all the salt it can.
Then leave it to **cool slowly**, and blue **crystals** grow.
Filter off the crystals, **dry** them, and you have pure copper sulfate.
It works with a **metal** or a **carbonate** too: add it until the **fizzing stops** and some solid is left over.

chapters.title: Recap: memory hooks and exam traps

lines.cap: Let's lock it all in.
**Please Stop Calling Me A Zebra, Instead Call Some Gold**: the reactivity series, from potassium down to gold.
**Red Bottoms, Blue Roofs**: litmus is **red** in acid and **blue** in alkali.
**Pop = Hydrogen, Milky = CO₂.**
And **A-B-S-W**: **acid + base → salt + water**.
Now, five exam traps to avoid.
One: acid + metal gives **hydrogen**. Only carbonates give **carbon dioxide**.
Two: neutralisation always makes **water**, as well as the salt.
Three: not all bases are alkalis. Only **soluble** bases are.
Four: **concentration** isn't **strength**. A dilute strong acid can be safer than a concentrated weak acid.
Five: **copper**, **silver** and **gold** don't fizz with dilute acids. They're **below hydrogen**.
Quick-fire quiz! Say each answer out loud before it appears.
What colour does litmus paper turn in an acid?
It turns **red**.
A solution has a pH of 12. Is it acidic, neutral or alkaline?
**Alkaline.** It's well above 7.
Which gas fizzes off when an acid reacts with a carbonate?
**Carbon dioxide**, which turns **limewater milky**.
An iron nail goes into blue copper sulfate solution. What happens?
The iron **displaces** the copper: the blue fades, and **copper** coats the nail.
Which salt do zinc and sulfuric acid make?
**Zinc sulfate**, not sulfide. Plus hydrogen gas.
Brilliant work. Now try the Acids, Bases & Metals quiz in your Science Lab, to lock it in.
